description.en: Acids are substances which increase the acidity of a foodstuff and/or impart a sour taste to it.
Acidity regulators are substances which alter or control the acidity or alkalinity of a foodstuff.
Added sugar is an ingredient that describes anything that counts as sugar.

Agave syrup -or agave nectar- is a liquid sweetener extracted from the core of the agave plant, particularly Agave tequilana, with production centered in Mexico where the plant has long been used to make traditional sweeteners and beverages like pulque. It has a mild, neutral sweetness—often noted as sweeter than honey—with subtle caramel notes in darker varieties, and a thin, smooth, honey-like texture that dissolves easily in cold liquids. Popular as a vegan honey substitute in beverages, baking, and dressings, agave syrup is very high in fructose -often 70-90%-, giving it a low glycemic index despite being calorie-dense, though its fructose concentration has raised similar metabolic concerns as high-fructose corn syrup.

ALLSPICE, also known as Jamaica pepper, myrtle pepper, pimenta, or pimento, is the dried unripe berry of Pimenta dioica, a midcanopy tree native to the Greater Antilles, southern Mexico, and Central America, now cultivated in many warm parts of the world.

The almond -Prunus amygdalus, syn. Prunus dulcis- is a species of tree native to Iran and surrounding countries, but widely cultivated elsewhere. The almond is also the name of the edible and widely cultivated seed of this tree.
Anti-caking agents are substances which reduce the tendency of individual particles of a foodstuff to adhere to one another.
Antioxidants are substances which prolong the shelf-life of foods by protecting them against deterioration caused by oxidation, such as fat rancidity and colour changes.

Apricots are stone fruits believed to have originated in China or Central Asia thousands of years ago, later spreading along the Silk Road through Persia and into the Mediterranean, where regions like Turkey and California became major modern producers. They have a delicate, sweet-tart flavor with subtle floral and honeyed notes, and a soft, velvety-skinned flesh that's juicy when ripe and firms into a chewy, concentrated sweetness when dried. Eaten fresh, dried, or used in jams, baking, and savory glazes, apricots are a good source of vitamin A -from beta-carotene-, vitamin C, and fiber, with dried apricots also offering a notable concentration of iron and potassium.

Arrowroot -Maranta arundinacea- is a tropical plant native to the Caribbean and Central/South America. It's a rhizome — an underground stem, similar in concept to ginger or turmeric. Arrowroot is most famous as a starch/thickener rather than a table vegetable.
Balsamic vinegar is a very dark, concentrated, and intensely flavoured vinegar originating in Italy, made wholly or partially from grape must, grape juice with all the skins, seeds and stems.

Bananas are tropical fruits believed to have originated in Southeast Asia and Papua New Guinea thousands of years ago, later spreading through Africa and eventually the Americas, where they became one of the world's most widely consumed and traded fruits. They have a sweet, mild, slightly tangy flavor with a soft, creamy texture that ripens from starchy and firm to soft and sugary as the fruit matures. Eaten fresh, cooked, or dried, and used in baking, smoothies, and desserts, bananas are notably rich in potassium, vitamin B6, and fiber, along with natural sugars that make them a popular quick energy source.
barley -hordeum vulgare-, a member of the grass family, is a major cereal grain grown in temperate climates globally

Barley flour or meal is made by grinding whole or pearled barley grains into a fine -flour- or coarse -meal- powder. Good source of dietary fiber, especially beta-glucan -a soluble fiber linked to cholesterol and blood sugar benefits-, provides B vitamins, selenium, and manganese.
A BEAN is a seed of one of several genera of the flowering plant family Fabaceae, which are used for human or animal food.
BEETROOT is the taproot portion of the beet plant

The bell pepper -also known as sweet pepper, pepper or capsicum /ˈkæpsɪkəm/- is a cultivar group of the species Capsicum annuum. Cultivars of the plant produce fruits in different colours, including red, yellow, orange, green, white, and purple.

Berries are small, fleshy, typically sweet-tart fruits produced by a wide range of flowering plants, growing wild across temperate and cold regions worldwide long before cultivation, with varieties like strawberries, blueberries, raspberries, and blackberries becoming widely farmed staples in Europe and North America. They have a flavor ranging from intensely sweet to sharply tart, often balanced with floral or earthy notes, and a soft, juicy texture that varies from the delicate burst of raspberries to the firmer bite of blueberries. Eaten fresh, dried, or used in jams, baking, and beverages, berries are notably rich in antioxidants -especially anthocyanins-, fiber, and vitamin C, making them among the most nutrient-dense fruits.

BIFIDOBACTERIUM ANIMALIS is a gram-positive, anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium of the Bifidobacterium genus which can be found in the large intestines of humans. Both old names B. animalis and B. lactis are still used on product labels, as this species is frequently used as a probiotic. In most cases, which subspecies is used in the product is not clear. Several companies have attempted to trademark particular strains, and as a marketing technique, have invented scientific-sounding names for the strains.
BIFIDOBACTERIUM is a genus of gram-positive, nonmotile, often branched anaerobic bacteria. They are ubiquitous inhabitants of the gastrointestinal tract, vagina and mouth of mammals humans.
A BISCUIT is a flour-based baked food product, which is typically hard, flat and unleavened.

Blue cheese or bleu cheese is cheese made with cultures of the mold Penicillium, giving it spots or veins of the mold throughout the cheese, which can vary in color through various shades of blue and green.
The Brazil nut -Bertholletia excelsa- is a South American tree in the family Lecythidaceae, and it is also the name of the tree's commercially harvested edible seeds.
Vicia faba, also known in the culinary sense as the broad bean, fava bean, or faba bean is a species of flowering plant in the pea and bean family Fabaceae.

Brown sugar is sugar—typically from sugarcane—that retains or has molasses added back in during processing, a practice with roots in unrefined "raw" sugars historically produced across the Caribbean, South Asia, and other cane-growing regions before fully refined white sugar became standard. It has a rich, warm, caramel-like flavor with subtle toffee and mineral notes from the molasses, and a moist, clumping texture ranging from light to dark depending on molasses content. Commonly used in baking, glazes, and sauces for its depth and moisture, brown sugar offers only trace minerals like calcium and iron from the molasses, making it nutritionally almost identical to white sugar—still primarily empty calories.

Buckwheat, despite its name, isn't a wheat relative at all—it's a fruit seed related to rhubarb, originating in Central Asia and cultivated in China for thousands of years before spreading through Europe and Russia. Its groats have an earthy, nutty flavor with a slight bitterness that deepens when toasted -as in kasha-, and they're used whole, ground into flour, or sprouted in dishes ranging from soba noodles to porridge and pancakes. Naturally gluten-free, buckwheat is a good source of plant protein, fiber, magnesium, and manganese, plus rutin, an antioxidant linked to cardiovascular benefits.
Bulking agents are substances which contribute to the volume of a foodstuff without contributing significantly to its available energy value.

BUTTER is a dairy product with high butterfat content which is solid when chilled and at room temperature in some regions, and liquid when warmed. It is made by churning fresh or fermented cream or milk to separate the butterfat from the buttermilk. It is generally used as a spread on plain or toasted bread products and a condiment on cooked vegetables, as well as in cooking, such as baking, sauce making, and pan frying.
BUTTERFAT - the fatty portion of milk.
BUTTERMILK was the liquid left behind after churning butter out of cultured cream.

Since the 6th century BC, cane sugar producers have crushed the harvested vegetable material from sugarcane in order to collect and filter the juice. They then treat the liquid -often with lime -calcium oxide-- to remove impurities and then neutralize it. Boiling the juice then allows the sediment to settle to the bottom for dredging out, while the scum rises to the surface for skimming off.

Canola oil, or canola for short, originally known as low erucic acid rapeseed, is a vegetable oil derived from a variety of rapeseed bred in Canada -Saskatchewan and Manitoba, 1960s-1970s- to be low in erucic acid, as opposed to colza oil.

Carnitine is a quaternary ammonium compound involved in metabolism in most mammals, plants and some bacteria. The body synthesizes enough carnitine from lysine side chains to keep up with the needs of energy production in the body as carnitine acts as a transporter of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria to be oxidized and produce energy. Food sources rich in L-carnitine are animal products such as meat, poultry, fish, and milk. Redder meats tend to have higher levels of L-carnitine. Some individuals with genetic or medical disorders -like preterm infants- cannot make enough, so this makes carnitine a conditionally essential nutrient for them.

Carob pods are mildly sweet on their own, so they are used in powdered, chip or syrup form as an ingredient in cakes and cookies, sometimes as a substitute for chocolate in recipes because of the color, texture, and taste of carob.
The CARROT -Daucus carota subsp. sativus- is a root vegetable, usually orange in colour, though purple, black, red, white, and yellow cultivars exist

Caseinate is a soluble form of casein—typically sodium or calcium caseinate—created by treating milk casein with an alkali to make it water-soluble, a processing method developed in the early-to-mid 20th century to allow casein's functional properties to be used more easily in manufactured foods. It has a neutral, mildly milky flavor with no strong aroma, and unlike regular casein, it dissolves smoothly in liquids and forms stable emulsions rather than clumping into curds. Widely used as an emulsifier and protein fortifier in coffee creamers, processed cheeses, and protein supplements, caseinate remains a complete protein containing all nine essential amino acids, along with calcium and phosphorus from its dairy origin.
Cinnamomum cassia, called Chinese cassia or Chinese cinnamon, is an evergreen tree originating in southern China
CAULIFLOWER is one of several vegetables in the species Brassica oleracea in the genus Brassica
The CAYENNE PEPPER is a type of Capsicum annuum. It is usually a moderately hot chili pepper used to flavor dishes.
CELERY -Apium graveolens- is a marshland plant in the family Apiaceae that has been cultivated as a vegetable since antiquity.
CHEDDAR cheese is a relatively hard, off-white, sometimes sharp-tasting, natural cheese.
CHEESE is a dairy product derived from milk that is produced in a wide range of flavors, textures, and forms by coagulation of the milk protein casein.
SALVIA HISPANICA, commonly known as CHIA, is a species of flowering plant in the mint family, Lamiaceae

Native to Mexico and Guatemala, chia seeds come from the flowering plant Salvia hispanica. Black seeds are the traditional, more widely available variety; white seeds are a naturally occurring lighter variant, often prized for their appearance in pale-colored dishes. Both share a mild, nutty flavor and neutral taste, absorbing surrounding flavors easily. When soaked, they develop a gel-like texture, making them ideal for puddings, smoothies, baked goods, and as an egg substitute. Nutritionally identical, both are rich in fiber, plant-based omega-3s, protein, calcium, and antioxidants — a versatile, nutrient-dense addition to any diet.

Chickpeas -Cicer arietinum-, also known as garbanzo beans, are one of the world's oldest cultivated legumes, originating in the Middle East over 7‚000 years ago and now grown widely across the Mediterranean, India, and the Americas. They have a mild, slightly nutty, earthy flavor with a firm yet creamy texture once cooked, making them extremely versatile in the kitchen. Chickpeas star in dishes like hummus, falafel, curries, soups, salads, and roasted snacks, and can be ground into flour for flatbreads and fritters. Nutritionally, they're a powerhouse: rich in plant-based protein, fiber, complex carbohydrates, iron, folate, and manganese, while being naturally low in fat. Their high fiber and protein content supports digestion, blood sugar stability, and satiety, making chickpeas a staple for vegetarian, vegan, and heart-healthy diets worldwide.

Choline chloride is an organic compound containing both quaternary ammonium salt and an alcohol. It is an important additive in feed especially for chickens where it accelerates growth. The US Food and Drug Administration requires that infant formula not made from cow's milk be supplemented with choline. Choline-providing dietary supplement ingredients include: choline chloride, choline bitartrate, citicoline -CDP-choline-, L-alpha-glycerophosphocholine -Alpha-GPC-, lecithin, phosphatidylcholine.

Modified citrus pectin -also known as CITRUS PECTIN, Pecta-Sol and MCP- is a modified, more digestible form of pectin. It is obtained from the peels, seeds and pulp of citrus fruits using a chemical extraction process.
CLOVEs are the aromatic flower buds of a tree in the family Myrtaceae, Syzygium aromaticum.

Cocoa comes from the seeds -beans- of the cacao tree, native to Central and South America and used by the Aztecs and Maya for thousands of years in ceremonial and medicinal drinks long before it spread to Europe in the 16th century and became the basis for modern chocolate. It has a rich, bitter, complex flavor with earthy, fruity, and slightly astringent notes that vary by origin and processing, and comes in forms ranging from raw beans and nibs to fine cocoa powder, defined by its fat content -cocoa butter- after pressing. Used in chocolate-making, baking, and beverages, cocoa is notably rich in flavanol antioxidants, along with magnesium, iron, and fiber, though its bitter compounds are often offset with added sugar in most commercial products.

COCOA BUTTER is a pale-yellow, edible vegetable fat extracted from the cocoa bean. Cocoa butter is a major ingredient in practically all types of chocolates -white chocolate, milk chocolate, and dark chocolate-.

name.en: cocoa powder with reduced cocoa butter content

description.en: COCONUT OIL, or copra oil, is an edible oil extracted from the kernel or meat of mature coconuts harvested from the coconut palm -Cocos nucifera-.

COCONUT SUGAR is a palm sugar produced from the sap of the flower bud stem of the coconut palm. It is used in savory dishes, but mainly in local desserts and cakes of the Southeast Asian region. Coconut sugar is subtly sweet almost like brown sugar but with a slight hint of caramel. The flavor and sweetness is usually similar to table sugar or brown sugar. There is no scientific evidence that coconut sugar is more nutritious or healthier than any other sweetener.

COLLAGEN is the main structural protein in the extracellular space in the various connective tissues in the body.  It is widely used in the form of collagen casings for sausages, which are also used in the manufacture of musical strings.

Colours are substances which add or restore colour in a food, and include natural constituents of foods and natural sources which are normally not consumed as foods as such and not normally used as characteristic ingredients of food.
Colza oil or colza is a non-drying oil obtained from the seeds of rapeseed -Brassica napus subsp. napus-.
CONCENTRATE is the form of substance which has had the majority of its base component -in the case of a liquid: the solvent- removed

Corn flour comes from maize, a grain domesticated in southern Mexico around 9‚000 years ago and later becoming a dietary cornerstone across the Americas, from Mexican tortillas to Southern U.S. cornbread. It has a mild, slightly sweet, distinctly corn flavor with a fine, slightly gritty texture that lends baked goods a tender crumb and golden color. Naturally gluten-free, corn flour offers decent fiber and is a good source of B vitamins and antioxidants like lutein and zeaxanthin, though its protein is incomplete and lower in quality compared to grains like quinoa.
Corn oil -maize oil- is oil extracted from the germ of corn -maize-.
Corn starch or maize starch is the starch derived from the corn -maize- grain.

Cottonseed is the seed of the cotton plant -genus Gossypium-, harvested as a byproduct of cotton fiber production. After cotton bolls are picked, the fluffy fiber -lint- is separated from the seeds during a process called ginning. Each cotton boll contains several seeds embedded in the fiber. Raw cottonseed contains a natural compound called gossypol, which is toxic to humans in significant quantities. Some specialty "glandless" cotton varieties have been bred to have naturally low gossypol levels, and these are sometimes explored as a protein source -the seed kernel is fairly protein-rich-, but this isn't mainstream or widely available commercially.
COTTONSEED OIL is a cooking oil extracted from the seeds of cotton plants of various species
COW MILK - raw cow milk that probably has been treated -pasteurisation-

Cranberries come in two main varieties: the American cranberry -Vaccinium macrocarpon-, native to North America and long used by Indigenous peoples before becoming a major commercial crop in states like Massachusetts and Wisconsin, and the smaller European cranberry -Vaccinium oxycoccos-, native to boggy regions across Northern Europe and Asia and traditionally foraged rather than farmed. Both have a sharply tart, astringent flavor with a firm, crisp bite when fresh, though the European variety tends to be smaller and even more tart than its larger American cousin. Eaten fresh, dried, juiced, or made into sauces, cranberries are notably rich in antioxidants, vitamin C, and compounds linked to urinary tract health, making them valued more for their functional benefits than their raw palatability.
CREAM is a dairy product composed of the higher-butterfat layer skimmed from the top of milk before homogenization.
DARK BLACK CHOCOLATE is a form of chocolate containing cocoa solids, cocoa butter and sugar, without the milk found in milk chocolate.

DATE, the fruit of the date palm -Phoenix dactylifera-. Dry or soft dates are eaten out-of-hand, or may be pitted and stuffed with fillings such as almonds, walnuts, pecans, candied orange and lemon peel, tahini, marzipan or cream cheese.
TARTRAZINE is a synthetic lemon yellow azo dye primarily used as a food coloring.

CARMINE, also called cochineal, cochineal extract, crimson lake or carmine lake, natural red 4, C.I. 75470, or E120, is a pigment of a bright-red color obtained from the aluminium salt of carminic acid
ERYTHROSINE, is an organoiodine compound, specifically a derivative of fluorone. It is cherry or melon-pink synthetic, primarily used for food coloring.

BRILLIANT BLUE FCF -Blue 1- is an organic compound classified as a blue triarylmethane dye, reflecting its chemical structure. Known under various commercial names, it is a colorant for foods and other substances.
CARAMEL is a medium to dark-orange confectionery product made by heating a variety of sugars.
Caramel color or caramel coloring is a water-soluble food coloring.

LUTEIN is a xanthophyll and one of 600 known naturally occurring carotenoids. Lutein is extracted from the petals of African marigold -Tagetes erecta-. It is approved for use in the EU and Australia and New Zealand. In the United States lutein may not be used as a food coloring for foods intended for human consumption, but can be added to animal feed.
CALCIUM CARBONATE is a chemical compound with the formula CaCO3.
SORBIC ACID, or 2‚4-hexadienoic acid, is a natural organic compound used as a food preservative. It has the chemical formula CH3-CH-4CO2H.
POTASSIUM SORBATE is the potassium salt of sorbic acid, chemical formula CH3CH=CH−CH=CH−CO2K.
SODIUM BENZOATE is a substance which has the chemical formula NaC7H5O2

Sulphur dioxide is a gas derived from burning elemental sulphur or as a byproduct of metal smelting and fossil fuel combustion. Industrially, it's produced by burning sulphur in oxygen or via the contact process used for sulphuric acid manufacturing. It has a sharp, pungent smell and, in concentrated form, a slightly acidic, irritating taste. In food, it acts as a preservative, antioxidant, and antimicrobial agent, commonly used in dried fruits, wine, fruit juices, and processed potatoes to prevent browning and spoilage. Nutritionally, it contributes no calories, vitamins, or minerals; it's regulated globally as a food additive with permitted maximum levels.
SODIUM METABISULFITE or sodium pyrosulfite -IUPAC spelling; Br. E. sodium metabisulphite or sodium pyrosulphite- is an inorganic compound of chemical formula Na2S2O5.
ACETIC ACID, systematically named ethanoic acid, is a colourless liquid organic compound with the chemical formula CH3COOH -also written as CH3CO2H or C2H4O2-.
SODIUM ACETATE, also abbreviated NaOAc,[8] is the sodium salt of acetic acid.

An organic acid naturally occurring in fermented foods, first identified in sour milk, now produced globally through microbial fermentation. It's manufactured by fermenting carbohydrate sources like corn, sugarcane, or beets with lactic acid bacteria, followed by purification. Lactic acid has a sharp, tangy, sour taste and is used worldwide as an acidulant, preservative, and pH regulator in dairy products, baked goods, beverages, pickled vegetables, and processed meats. It also aids fermentation in foods like yogurt and sauerkraut. Nutritionally, it provides a negligible caloric contribution and no significant vitamins or minerals, functioning primarily as a flavoring and preservation agent rather than a nutrient source.
Sodium propanoate or SODIUM PROPIONATE is the sodium salt of propionic acid.

CALCIUM PROPIONATE has the formula Ca-C2H5COO-2. Calcium propionate is used as a preservative in a wide variety of products, including but not limited to:bread, other baked goods, processed meat, whey, and other dairy products.
MALIC ACID is an organic compound with the molecular formula C4H6O5. Malic acid has two stereoisomeric forms -L- and D-enantiomers-, though only the L-isomer exists naturally.

Ascorbic acid is a naturally occurring organic compound found in citrus fruits, berries, and vegetables such as peppers and broccoli. Commercially, it is produced industrially through fermentation of glucose -often derived from corn-, followed by chemical conversion steps, yielding a highly pure, food-grade powder. It has a mildly tart, sour taste, similar to citrus. Ascorbic acid is widely used as a food additive -E300- for its antioxidant properties, preventing browning and preserving freshness in juices, canned goods, and processed foods. Nutritionally, it is an essential water-soluble vitamin, contributing to collagen synthesis, immune function, and iron absorption across diverse global diets.
SODIUM ASCORBATE is one of a number of mineral salts of ascorbic acid -vitamin C-.
ASCORBYL PALMITATE is an ester formed from ascorbic acid and palmitic acid creating a fat-soluble form of vitamin C.

is a generic term to designate any group of yellow-brownish fatty substances occurring in animal and plant tissues, and are used for smoothing food textures, dissolving powders -emulsifying-, homogeLECITHINnizing liquid mixtures, and repelling sticking materials. The term lecithin refers to a group of compounds found in every living organism, as they are part of the cell wall of all cells. Lecithin is commercially isolated -mainly- from soybeans or egg yolk.
POTASSIUM BITARTRATE, also known as potassium hydrogen tartrate, with formula KC4H5O6, is a byproduct of winemaking.
SODIUM PHOSPHATES is a generic term for a variety of salts of sodium -Na+- and phosphate -PO43−-.

description.en: DISODIUM PHOSPHATE, or sodium hydrogen phosphate, or sodium phosphate dibasic, is the inorganic compound with the formula Na2HPO4.

additives_classes.en: en:emulsifier, en:humectant, en:preservative, en:sequestrant, en:stabiliser, en:thickener

description.en: TRISODIUM PHOSPHATE is the inorganic compound with the chemical formula Na3PO4.

additives_classes.en: en:emulsifier, en:humectant, en:preservative, en:sequestrant, en:stabiliser, en:thickener

description.en: Derived from Rosmarinus officinalis, a Mediterranean evergreen shrub cultivated widely across Europe, North Africa, and increasingly in Asia and the Americas. The extract is produced by drying rosemary leaves and processing them through solvent or CO₂ extraction to isolate concentrated compounds, primarily carnosic acid and rosmarinic acid. It carries a robust, herbaceous flavor with piney, slightly peppery, and mildly bitter notes. Commonly used as a natural antioxidant and preservative in processed meats, oils, snacks, and sauces, it helps extend shelf life by slowing oxidation. Nutritionally, rosemary extract contains trace polyphenols and antioxidant compounds, though it's typically used in amounts too small to contribute meaningfully to daily nutrient intake.

additives_classes.en: en:carrier, en:emulsifier, en:humectant, en:sequestrant, en:stabiliser, en:thickener

description.en: GUM ARABIC, also known as acacia gum, arabic gum, gum acacia, acacia, Senegal gum and Indian gum
XANTHAN GUM is a polysaccharide with many industrial uses, including as a common food additive.
SODIUM ACID PYROPHOSPHATE is an additive used to prevent the formation of crystals and discoloration of the crab meat.

CELLULOSE is an organic compound with the formula -C6H10O5-n, a polysaccharide consisting of a linear chain of several hundred to many thousands of linked D-glucose units. Cellulose is used as emulsifier, thickener and stabilizer in processed foods. Cellulose powder is, for example, used in processed cheese to prevent caking inside the package.
METHYL CELLULOSE is a chemical compound derived from cellulose. Methyl cellulose is added to food products, to generate their characteristic thick consistency, for example ice cream or croquette.
MONO- AND DIGLYCERIDES OF FATTY ACIDS -E471- refers to a food additive composed of diglycerides and monoglycerides which is used as an emulsifier.
SODIUM CARBONATES is the generic term for a Na and CO3 combination.
SODIUM BICARBONATE -sodium hydrogen carbonate-, commonly known as baking soda, is a chemical compound with the formula NaHCO3.

AMMONIUM CARBONATE is a salt with the chemical formula -NH4-2CO3. Since it readily degrades to gaseous ammonia and carbon dioxide upon heating, it is used as a leavening agent. It is also known as baker's ammonia and was a predecessor to the more modern leavening agents baking soda and baking powder.

AMMONIUM BICARBONATE is an inorganic compound with formula -NH4-HCO3, simplified to NH5CO3. Ammonium bicarbonate is used in the food industry as a raising agent for flat baked goods, such as cookies and crackers, and in China in steamed buns and Chinese almond cookies. It was commonly used in the home before modern day baking powder was made available.
MAGNESIUM CARBONATE, MgCO3 -archaic name magnesia alba-, is an inorganic salt that is a white solid.
MONOSODIUM GLUTAMATE -MSG, also known as sodium glutamate- is the sodium salt of glutamic acid, one of the most abundant naturally occurring non-essential amino acids.
Sodium saccharin -benzoic sulfimide- is an artificial sweetener with effectively no food energy.

MALTITOL is a sugar alcohol -a polyol- used as a sugar substitute. It has 75–90% of the sweetness of sucrose -table sugar- and nearly identical properties, except for browning. Maltitol's high sweetness allows it to be used without being mixed with other sweeteners. It is used in candy manufacture, particularly sugar-free hard candy, chewing gum, chocolates, baked goods, and ice cream.
EGGS are laid by female animals of many different species, including birds, reptiles, amphibians, mammals, and fish. This ingredient comprises mainly chicken eggs.
EGG WHITE is the clear liquid -also called the albumen or the glair/glaire- contained within an egg.
Emulsifiers are substances which make it possible to form or maintain a homogenous mixture of two or more immiscible phases such as oil and water in a foodstuff.
ENZYME - is a macromolecular biological catalysts. Enzymes accelerate chemical reactions.
An extract is a substance made by extracting a part of a raw material, often by using a solvent such as ethanol or water. Extracts may be sold as tinctures, absolutes or in powder form.
FAT is one of the three main macronutrients, along with the other two:carbohydrate and protein. Fats molecules consist of primarily carbon and hydrogen atoms, thus they are all hydrocarbon molecules.
FERMENT is an agent, such as an enzyme, bacterium, or fungus, that brings about fermentation.
IRONII PHOSPHATE, Fe3-PO4-2, is an iron salt of phosphoric acid.

IronIII phosphate, also ferric phosphate, is the inorganic compound with the formula FePO4. Iron-III- phosphate is not allowed as food additive in the European Union. It was withdrawn from the list of allowed substances in the directive 2002/46/EC in 2007.

IRONII SULFATE denotes a range of salts with the formula FeSO4·xH2O. The hydrated form is used medically to treat iron deficiency. It is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines, the most important medications needed in a basic health system.

Dietary fiber is the indigestible carbohydrate portion of plant foods, produced worldwide from cereals -oats, wheat, rice-, legumes -peas, soy-, fruits -citrus, apple-, roots -chicory, sugar beet- and sugarcane residues. Production involves collecting by-products or plant parts, washing, extracting or milling, drying, and sometimes bleaching or purifying to a fine powder. Its taste is neutral to slightly sweet or grainy. Industries use it to add bulk, retain moisture, thicken, replace fat or sugar, and improve texture in bakery, meat, dairy, and beverage products. Nutritionally, it provides little to no digestible energy -0 to 2 kcal/g-, and can be soluble or insoluble.
Firming agents are substances which make or keep tissues of fruit or vegetables firm or crisp, or interact with gelling agents to produce or strengthen a gel.
FISH OIL is oil derived from the tissues of oily fish
Flavour enhancers are substances which enhance the existing taste and/or odour of a foodstuff.
Flax, also known as common flax or linseed, is a flowering plant, Linum usitatissimum, in the family Linaceae. Flax seeds occur in two basic varieties/colors: brown or yellow -golden linseeds-.
FLOUR is a powder made by grinding raw grains or roots and used to make many different foods.
Flour treatment agents are substances, other than emulsifiers, which are added to flour or dough to improve its baking quality.

Fructooligosaccharide -FOS- is a short-chain fructan found naturally in foods like chicory root, onions, garlic, and bananas, and produced commercially either by extracting it from chicory or through enzymatic conversion of sucrose, with much of the technology developed in Japan and France. It has a mild sweetness, roughly 30-50% as sweet as sucrose, with a clean flavor and no notable aroma, and is used in food products as a low-calorie sweetener, texture enhancer, and fat replacer. Like oligofructose, FOS acts as a soluble prebiotic fiber that resists digestion in the small intestine and ferments in the colon to feed beneficial gut bacteria, providing fewer calories than sucrose while supporting digestive health.

Fructose is a simple sugar -monosaccharide- that occurs naturally in fruits, honey, and some vegetables, and is produced commercially either by processing corn starch into high-fructose corn syrup -mainly in the U.S.- or by refining it from sucrose. It has the sweetest taste of all natural sugars—notably sweeter than sucrose or glucose—with no notable aroma, and is used in beverages, baked goods, and processed foods both for its intense sweetness and its ability to enhance flavor and browning. Fructose provides purely empty calories with no fiber, vitamins, or minerals, and is metabolized differently than glucose—processed primarily by the liver—which has made it a focus of concern around excessive consumption and links to metabolic issues.

Fruit is the mature, seed-bearing structure of flowering plants, cultivated and foraged by humans since prehistoric times across virtually every inhabited region, with different varieties native to tropical, temperate, and Mediterranean climates worldwide. It has an enormously varied flavor and texture profile—from the crisp sweetness of apples to the juicy tang of citrus and the soft, custardy richness of tropical fruits like mango—generally balancing natural sugars with acidity. Eaten fresh, dried, juiced, or cooked into jams, desserts, and savory dishes, fruit is prized nutritionally for its fiber, vitamins -especially vitamin C-, antioxidants, and natural sugars, making it a nutrient-dense counterpart to refined sweeteners.
Gelling agents are substances which give a foodstuff texture through formation of a gel.
GINGER -Zingiber officinale- is a flowering plant whose rhizome, ginger root or simply ginger, is widely used as a spice or a folk medicine
Glazing agents -including lubricants- are substances which, when applied to the external surface of a foodstuff, impart a shiny appearance or provide a protective coating.

Glucose is a simple sugar -monosaccharide- that occurs naturally in fruits, honey, and plants, and is produced commercially by breaking down starch—typically from corn in the U.S. or wheat and potatoes in Europe—through enzymatic or acid hydrolysis. It has a moderately sweet flavor, less sweet than sucrose or fructose, with no notable aroma, and is available as a syrup or dried/powdered form used widely in candy-making, baking, and brewing for its resistance to crystallization and browning properties. As the primary fuel source for the human body, glucose provides purely caloric energy with no fiber, vitamins, or minerals, and it's the sugar that directly raises blood glucose levels, giving it the highest glycemic index among common sugars.
A grape is a fruit, botanically a berry, of the deciduous woody vines of the flowering plant genus Vitis.
Grape juice is obtained from crushing and blending grapes into a liquid.
This is a compound product made of concentrate grape juice and water.
The HAZELNUT is the nut of the hazel and therefore includes any of the nuts deriving from species of the genus Corylus, especially the nuts of the species Corylus avellana.
High-fructose corn syrup -HFCS- -also called glucose-fructose, isoglucose and glucose-fructose syrup- is a sweetener made from corn starch
HONEY is a sweet, viscous food substance produced by bees and some related insects.

Humectants are substances which prevent foods from drying out by counteracting the effect of an atmosphere having a low degree of humidity, or promote the dissolution of a powder in an aqueous medium.

Hydrogenation converts liquid vegetable oils into solid or semi-solid fats, such as those present in margarine. Changing the degree of saturation of the fat changes some important physical properties, such as the melting range, which is why liquid oils become semi-solid.

Hydrolyzed vegetable protein -HVP- is a flavor enhancer made by chemically breaking down plant proteins—typically soy, corn, or wheat—using acid hydrolysis, a process developed in the early 20th century and widely adopted in industrial food manufacturing to create savory, meat-like flavors without meat. It has an intensely savory, umami-rich flavor with notes reminiscent of broth or bouillon, and comes as a fine powder or paste used in tiny quantities to boost taste. Commonly used in soups, sauces, snack seasonings, and processed foods as a cheaper alternative to natural flavor development, HVP contributes free glutamic acid -similar to MSG- along with trace amino acids, but is used in such small amounts that it offers negligible nutritional value beyond flavor enhancement.

INOSITOL is a carbocyclic sugar that is abundant in brain and other mammalian tissues, mediates cell signal transduction and participates in osmoregulation. It is a sugar alcohol with half the sweetness of table sugar. It is made naturally in humans from glucose. A human kidney will produce around two grams each day. Foods containing the highest concentrations of inositol include fruits, beans, grains, and nuts.

INULINS are a group of naturally occurring polysaccharides produced by many types of plants, industrially most often extracted from chicory. Chicory root is the main source of extraction for commercial production of inulin. It can be used to replace sugar, fat, and flour.

Invert sugar is a liquid sugar syrup produced by splitting sucrose into its component parts—glucose and fructose—through hydrolysis using heat, acid, or enzymes, a process discovered in the 19th century and now widely used in food manufacturing rather than home kitchens. It has a flavor sweeter than regular sugar -since fructose tastes sweeter than sucrose- with a smooth, syrupy texture, and it's prized in baking and confectionery for resisting crystallization, retaining moisture, and extending shelf life in products like candies, jams, and soft baked goods. Like other sugars, invert sugar provides purely empty calories with no meaningful vitamins, minerals, or fiber, offering energy without nutritional value.
IODINE is a chemical element with symbol I and atomic number 53.
IODISED SALT - is salt mixed with a minute amount of various salts of the element iodine.

IRON is a chemical element with symbol Fe -from Latin:ferrum- and atomic number 26. Iron is pervasive, but particularly rich sources of dietary iron include red meat, oysters, lentils, beans, poultry, fish, leaf vegetables, watercress, tofu, chickpeas, black-eyed peas, and blackstrap molasses. Iron provided by dietary supplements is often found as ironII fumarate, although iron-II- sulfate is cheaper and is absorbed equally well.

Jalapeño peppers are probably the most familiar chili in American and Mexican cooking — a good middle-ground pepper for both flavor and heat. The taste is grassy, slightly sweet, and vegetal with a clean, building heat.

Juice is the liquid extracted from fruits or vegetables, produced by pressing, squeezing, or blending, with a history stretching back to ancient civilizations that fermented or drank fruit juices, though modern commercial juicing scaled up dramatically in the 20th century with pasteurization and packaging advances. It has a flavor that mirrors its source—sweet, tart, or a mix—with a smooth, liquid texture, sometimes with pulp retained for added body. Consumed as a beverage or used in cooking, baking, and cocktails, juice retains vitamins -especially vitamin C- and antioxidants from its source, though it typically lacks the fiber of whole fruit and can be concentrated in natural sugars, giving it a higher glycemic impact than eating the fruit whole.

KETCHUP is a sauce used as a condiment. Ketchup is a sweet and tangy sauce now typically made from tomatoes, sugar, and vinegar, with assorted seasonings and spices. The specific spices and flavors vary, but commonly include onions, allspice, coriander, cloves, cumin, garlic, and mustard; and sometimes include celery, cinnamon or ginger.

L-CARNITINE is the left isomer of carnitine, a quaternary ammonium compound involved in metabolism in most mammals, plants and some bacteria. The body synthesizes enough carnitine from lysine side chains to keep up with the needs of energy production in the body as carnitine acts as a transporter of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria to be oxidized and produce energy. Food sources rich in L-carnitine are animal products such as meat, poultry, fish, and milk. Redder meats tend to have higher levels of L-carnitine. Some individuals with genetic or medical disorders -like preterm infants- cannot make enough, so this makes carnitine a conditionally essential nutrient for them.

LACTASE is essential to the complete digestion of whole milk; it breaks down lactose, a sugar which gives milk its sweetness. Lactase is an enzyme that some people are unable to produce in their small intestine.[5] Without it they can't break down the natural lactose in milk. Lactase produced commercially can be extracted both from yeasts such as Kluyveromyces fragilis and Kluyveromyces lactis and from molds, such as Aspergillus niger and Aspergillus oryzae.

Lactic acid bacteria -LAB- are an order of gram-positive, low-GC, acid-tolerant, generally nonsporulating, nonrespiring, either rod-shaped -bacilli- or spherical -cocci- bacteria that share common metabolic and physiological characteristics.

LACTOBACILLUS is a genus of Gram-positive, facultative anaerobic or microaerophilic, rod-shaped, non-spore-forming bacteria. Lactobacillus is the most common probiotic found in food such as yogurt, and it is diverse in its application to maintain human well-being. Some Lactobacillus species are used as starter cultures in industry for controlled fermentation in the production of wine, yogurt, cheese, sauerkraut, pickles, beer, cider, kimchi, cocoa, kefir, and other fermented foods.

LACTOBACILLUS ACIDOPHILUS is a species of gram positive bacteria in the genus Lactobacillus. L. acidophilus is a homofermentative, microaerophilic species, fermenting sugars into lactic acid. These strains are commercially used in many dairy products in the production of acidophilus-type yogurt.
LACTOBACILLUS DELBRUECKII SUBSP. BULGARICUS -until 2014 known as Lactobacillus bulgaricus- is the main bacteria used for the production of yogurt.
LACTOBACILLUS CASEI is a species of genus Lactobacillus found in the human urinary tract and mouth. The most common application of L. casei is industrial, specifically for dairy production.

A LEGUME is a plant in the family Fabaceae -or Leguminosae-, or the fruit or seed of such a plant -also called a pulse-. Legumes are grown agriculturally, primarily for human consumption. Grain legumes include beans, lentils, lupins, peas, and peanuts.
The skin or outer layer of a lemon.

Originating in the Fertile Crescent over 8‚000 years ago, lentils spread across the Mediterranean, Middle East, South Asia, and beyond, becoming a dietary cornerstone worldwide. Known as "dal" in South Asia, they come in many varieties—red, green, brown, black, yellow—each with subtly different flavor, from mild and sweet to earthy. Quick-cooking and hulling-friendly, lentils are simmered into soups, stews, curries, and purées across cuisines, from Indian dal tadka to French lentille du Puy salads and Middle Eastern mujadara. Nutritionally, they're a powerhouse of plant protein, fiber, iron, and folate, making them a global staple for sustainable, affordable nutrition.

Lupin or lupini beans are the yellow legume seeds of the genus Lupinus. They are traditionally eaten as a pickled snack food. The lupin is devoid of starch, which is very unusual for a species of edible bean. Lupin allergy may cause life-threatening anaphylaxis in sensitive individuals. Only "sweet" varieties of lupin are used for human food
Malt is germinated cereal grains that have been dried in a process known as "malting".

MANGANESE is a chemical element with symbol Mn and atomic number 25. Manganese is an essential human dietary element. It is present as a coenzyme in several biological processes, which include macronutrient metabolism, bone formation, free radical defense systems.
MANGANESE SULFATE usually refers to the inorganic compound with the formula MnSO4·H2O. Magnesium sulfate is used as a brewing salt in making beer. It may also be used as a coagulant for making tofu.
MARGARINE is a spread used for flavoring, baking, and cooking. Margarine is made mainly of refined vegetable oil and water.
MASCARPONE is an Italian cream cheese coagulated by the addition of certain acidic substances such as lemon juice, vinegar, citric acid or acetic acid.

A microbiological culture, or microbial culture, is a method of multiplying microbial organisms by letting them reproduce in predetermined culture medium under controlled laboratory conditions. All cultures in food are microbial cultures

Some molds such as Rhizomucor miehei are able to produce proteolytic enzymes. Cheeses produced this way are suitable for vegetarians, provided no animal-based alimentation was used during the production.
MILK - a white liquid nutrient-rich food produced by the mammary glands of mammals.
MILK CHOCOLATE is solid chocolate made with milk added in the form of powdered milk, liquid milk, or condensed milk.

Millet is an ancient cereal grain domesticated in East Asia and Africa thousands of years ago, historically a staple in China, India, and parts of Africa long before rice and wheat became dominant. It has a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor with a light, fluffy texture when cooked, and a firmer, chewier bite when toasted first. It's naturally gluten-free and used in porridges, pilafs, flatbreads, and baked goods, offering a solid source of magnesium, phosphorus, fiber, and plant protein, along with antioxidants.
Molasses -American English- or black treacle -British English- is a viscous product resulting from refining sugarcane or sugar beets into sugar.
Powder or paste made from seeds of the mustard plant, and used as a condiment or a spice.

name.en: natural raspberry flavouring with other natural flavourings
natural vanilla flavouring with other natural flavourings

description.en: NUTMEG is the seed or ground spice of several species of the genus Myristica.

Oats are a cereal grain that originated in Western Asia or Europe, historically used as animal fodder before rising to prominence as a hearty breakfast staple, especially in Scotland and Northern Europe. They have a mild, creamy, subtly sweet flavor with a soft, chewy texture that varies by processing—from firm steel-cut to quick-cooking rolled or instant forms. Oats are naturally gluten-free -though often cross-contaminated during processing- and are notable for their beta-glucan fiber, which supports heart health, along with solid amounts of protein, manganese, and iron.

Rolled oats are whole oat groats that have been steamed and pressed flat with large rollers, a processing method developed in the late 1800s to shorten cooking time while keeping the grain mostly intact. They have a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor with a soft, chewy texture that holds its shape better than instant oats, making them the classic choice for traditional oatmeal, granola, and baking. Like other oats, they're naturally gluten-free -if uncontaminated- and rich in beta-glucan fiber for heart health, plus protein, manganese, and iron, though their nutrition is nearly identical to whole oats since minimal processing preserves the bran and germ.

Cooking OIL is plant, animal, or synthetic fat used in frying, baking, and other types of cooking. It is also used in food preparation and flavouring not involving heat, such as salad dressings and bread dips, and in this sense might be more accurately termed edible oil.

Several edible vegetable and animal oils, and also fats, are used for various purposes in cooking and food preparation. In particular, many foods are fried in oil much hotter than boiling water. Oils are also used for flavoring and for modifying the texture of foods -e.g. Stir Fry-. Cooking oils are derived either from animal fat, as butter, lard and other types, or plant oils from the olive, maize, sunflower and many other species.

Oligofructose is a type of fructan—a short-chain fructose oligosaccharide—found naturally in plants like chicory root, onions, and bananas, and produced commercially mainly through partial enzymatic hydrolysis of chicory inulin, a process developed in Europe where chicory-based fibers are widely used. It has a mild sweetness, roughly 30-50% as sweet as sucrose, with a clean flavor and no notable aroma, and is used in food products as a low-calorie sweetener, fat replacer, and texture enhancer. Unlike simple sugars, oligofructose acts as a soluble prebiotic fiber that resists digestion in the small intestine and ferments in the colon, feeding beneficial gut bacteria while providing fewer calories than sucrose and supporting digestive health.
OLIVE OIL is a liquid fat obtained from olives -the fruit of Olea europaea-.
Orange juice is the liquid extract of the orange tree fruit, produced by squeezing oranges.
Oregano -Origanum vulgare- is a flowering plant in the mint family -Lamiaceae-.
the solid state of the vegetable oil, obtained from the fruit of oil palms.

PALM KERNEL OIL is an edible plant oil derived from the kernel of the oil palm Elaeis guineensis. It should not be confused with the other two edible oils derived from palm fruits:palm oil, extracted from the pulp of the oil palm fruit, and coconut oil, extracted from the kernel of the coconut.
PALM OIL is an edible vegetable oil derived from the mesocarp -reddish pulp- of the fruit of the oil palms
Palm stearin is the solid fraction of palm oil.
Pantothenic acid, also called vitamin B5 -a B vitamin-, is a water-soluble vitamin.
“Paprika” can be either the dried powder or the fruit of a plant in some languages. Put it only here if that is the case, otherwise put the ingredient under en:bell pepper or en:paprika.
PARMIGIANO-REGGIANO is an Italian hard, granular cheese.
PARSLEY or garden parsley -Petroselinum crispum- is a species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae
The PARSNIP -Pastinaca sativa- is a root vegetable closely related to the carrot and parsley.
Skimmed milk -British English- is made when all the cream is removed from whole milk. It tends to contain around 0.1% fat. Láit écrémé has a maximum of 0.5% fat.

Peas are a good example of how the same plant can fall into different categories depending on how it's harvested and used. Fresh peas -green peas, snap peas, snow peas- are harvested young and eaten fresh, in or out of the pod. they are classified as a vegetable, not a pulse. Dried peas are the same plant, but the peas are left to mature and dry on the vine before harvesting. This is what counts as a pulse.

The peach -Prunus persica- is a deciduous tree native to the region of Northwest China. It bears edible juicy fruits with various characteristics, most called peaches and others -the glossy-skinned varieties-, nectarines.
PEANUT OIL, also known as groundnut oil or arachis oil, is a mild-tasting vegetable oil derived from peanuts.
The PEAR is any of several tree and shrub species of genus Pyrus, in the family Rosaceae. Note this refers to the tree and not the fruit

Peppercorns and the ground pepper derived from them may be described simply as pepper, or more precisely as black pepper -cooked and dried unripe fruit-, green pepper -dried unripe fruit-, and white pepper -ripe fruit seeds-.

POTASSIUM IODIDE is a chemical compound, medication, and dietary supplement. As a medication it is used to treat hyperthyroidism, in radiation emergencies, and to protect the thyroid gland when certain types of radiopharmaceuticals are used.
The POTATO is a starchy, tuberous crop from the perennial nightshade Solanum tuberosum.
Potato starch is starch extracted from potatoes.
Poultry are domesticated birds kept by humans for their eggs, their meat or their feathers.

Preservatives are substances which prolong the shelf-life of foods by protecting them against deterioration caused by micro-organisms and/or which protect against growth of pathogenic micro-organisms.

Protein is a macronutrient made of amino acid chains, sourced from a wide range of foods—animal sources like meat, fish, eggs, and dairy, and plant sources like legumes, grains, nuts, and soy—with humans relying on food-derived protein since prehistoric times as one of the three core macronutrients alongside fats and carbohydrates. Its flavor and texture vary enormously by source, from the rich, savory taste of meats to the neutral, often bland profile of isolated protein powders, which are typically processed from whey, soy, or pea into fine, mixable forms. Essential for building and repairing muscle, enzymes, and hormones, protein is measured by its amino acid completeness—animal proteins and a few plant sources like quinoa and soy are "complete," containing all nine essential amino acids, while most other plant proteins must be combined to achieve the same profile.

Psyllium is the seed husk of Plantago ovata, grown mainly in India -the world's dominant producer-, with smaller output in Pakistan, Iran, and parts of Europe. Seeds are harvested, cleaned, and milled, then the husk is mechanically separated by sifting and air classification, and sometimes ground into powder. It is nearly tasteless, with a slightly mucilaginous texture. It is used as a binder and gelling agent in gluten-free baking, as a thickener, and in fiber supplements and cereals. Nutritionally, it is about 70 to 85% soluble fiber, providing roughly 0 to 2 kcal/g, with negligible fat and protein.

pulse = just the dry, harvested seed of specific legume crops. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization -FAO- recognizes 11 categories of pulses: Dry beans — includes kidney beans, navy beans, pinto beans, black beans, lima beans, mung beans, adzuki beans; Dry broad beans — fava beans, horse beans, broad beans -in dried form-; Dry peas — includes split peas, whole dried peas -green or yellow-; Chickpeas — also called garbanzo beans; Dry cowpeas — black-eyed peas, blackeye beans; Pigeon peas — also called Congo beans or gandules; Lentils — includes red, green, brown, black -beluga-, French -Puy-; Bambara beans — also called Bambara groundnuts -earth peas-; Vetches — common vetch; Lupins — lupin beans -also called lupini beans-; Minor pulses — a catch-all for less common ones, such as lablab, jack beans, winged beans, yam beans
A PUMPKIN is a cultivar of a squash plant, most commonly of Cucurbita pepo, that is round, with smooth, slightly ribbed skin, and deep yellow to orange coloration.

Quinoa is an ancient pseudocereal native to the Andean region of South America, cultivated by the Incas for thousands of years and revered as a sacred "mother grain." It has a light, slightly nutty and earthy flavor with a delicate crunch, and its grains form a small, curled tail when cooked that gives it a distinctive texture. Naturally gluten-free, quinoa is notable for being a complete protein containing all nine essential amino acids, and it's also a good source of fiber, iron, magnesium, and manganese.
A RAISIN is a dried grape.

Raising agents are substances added to baked goods to produce carbon dioxide gas and create rise and lightness, with early forms like yeast used since ancient Egyptian times, while chemical versions such as baking soda and baking powder were developed in the 19th century as faster, more reliable alternatives. They are essentially flavorless or very mildly bitter/metallic on their own, though excess use can leave a soapy or tinny aftertaste, and they work by releasing gas bubbles that get trapped in dough or batter, creating a light, airy texture. Used across breads, cakes, and pastries—commonly as baking soda, baking powder, yeast, or ammonium bicarbonate—raising agents are used in such small quantities that they contribute negligible calories or nutrients, functioning purely as a leavening tool rather than a nutritional ingredient.

Rapeseed -Brassica napus-, also known as rape, or oilseed rape, is a bright-yellow flowering member of the family Brassicaceae, cultivated mainly for its oil-rich seed, which naturally contains appreciable amounts of erucic acid. Rapeseed is the third-largest source of vegetable oil and the second-largest source of protein meal in the world.

Red rice is a whole-grain rice variety that gets its reddish-brown hue from anthocyanin pigments in its bran layer, with well-known types grown in regions like Thailand, Bhutan, and the Camargue in France. It has a robust, earthy, slightly nutty flavor with a chewy, hearty texture, since the bran layer is left intact rather than polished away as with white rice. Naturally gluten-free, red rice is notably richer in fiber, antioxidants, and minerals like iron and magnesium than white rice, thanks to that retained bran layer.
RENNET is a complex set of enzymes produced in the stomachs of ruminant mammals. Chymosin, its key component, is a protease enzyme that curdles the casein in milk.

Rice is a cereal grain domesticated independently in China and possibly India thousands of years ago, and it remains the staple food for over half the world's population, central to cuisines across Asia, Africa, and Latin America. It has a mild, subtly sweet flavor with a texture that varies widely by variety—from the fluffy separate grains of basmati to the sticky clumps of short-grain sushi rice. Naturally gluten-free, rice's nutrition depends heavily on processing: brown rice retains its bran and germ for fiber, B vitamins, magnesium, and manganese, while white rice is more refined and comparatively lower in nutrients.
Rice flour is a form of flour made from finely milled rice.
ROOT VEGETABLES are underground plant parts eaten by humans as food.

Rye is a cereal grain native to Southwest Asia and Eastern Europe, historically thriving in cold, poor soils where wheat struggled, making it a staple grain across Northern and Eastern Europe and Scandinavia. It has a bold, earthy, slightly sour and tangy flavor with a dense, hearty texture, most familiar in dark rye bread, pumpernickel, and crispbreads. Rye contains gluten -though less than wheat- and is valued for its high fiber content, particularly soluble fiber that supports blood sugar control, along with good levels of manganese, phosphorus, and B vitamins.
SALT - is a mineral composed primarily of sodium chloride -NaCl-, a chemical compound belonging to the larger class of salts "sodium chloride" is defined in minerals.txt
SEA SALT - is salt that is produced by the evaporation of seawater
SELENIUM is a chemical element with symbol Se and atomic number 34.
LAIT DEMI-ECREME has a butterfat percentage of 1.5-1.8% fat by regulation
Semolina is the coarse, purified wheat middlings of durum wheat mainly used in making pasta and couscous.

SHEA BUTTER is a fat extracted from the nut of the African shea tree -Vitellaria paradoxa-. Shea butter is edible and is used in food preparation in some African countries. Occasionally, shea butter is mixed with other oils as a substitute for cocoa butter, although the taste is noticeably different.
LOW-FAT MILK is a 1% fat milk, sold in the United States. Skim milk -American English-, is made when all the cream is removed from whole milk. It tends to contain around 0% fat.

SODIUM is a chemical element with symbol Na -from Latin natrium- and atomic number 11. In humans, sodium is an essential mineral that regulates blood volume, blood pressure, osmotic equilibrium and pH; the minimum physiological requirement for sodium is 500 milligrams per day.

SODIUM SELENITE is the inorganic compound with the formula Na2SeO3. Because selenium is an essential element, sodium selenite is an ingredient in dietary supplements such as multi-vitamin/mineral products.

SOUR CREAM is a dairy product obtained by fermenting regular cream with certain kinds of lactic acid bacteria. The bacterial culture, which is introduced either deliberately or naturally, sours and thickens the cream. Its name comes from the production of lactic acid by bacterial fermentation, which is called souring. Fat percentage is 18-20%.

Sourdough is a naturally leavened bread made using a fermented starter of wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria rather than commercial yeast, a method dating back thousands of years to ancient Egypt and still central to regional baking traditions like San Francisco's tangy loaves. It has a distinctive tangy, slightly sour flavor with a chewy, dense crumb and crisp, often blistered crust, shaped by the specific microbial culture of its starter, which can vary by region and even household. Made simply from flour, water, salt, and the starter culture, sourdough's slow fermentation is thought to improve digestibility and lower the glycemic impact compared to conventionally leavened bread, while offering fiber, B vitamins, and modest protein from the flour base.

Soy comes from the soybean, a legume domesticated in China around 3‚000-5‚000 years ago and long a dietary staple across East Asia, later spreading globally as both a food crop and major agricultural commodity. It has a mild, earthy, slightly nutty flavor with a texture that varies enormously by form—from the firm bite of tofu and edamame to the smooth creaminess of soy milk and the meaty chew of tempeh. Extremely versatile, soy is used in countless forms including tofu, milk, sauce, and protein isolates, and stands out nutritionally as a complete plant protein containing all nine essential amino acids, along with fiber, iron, and isoflavones linked to potential health benefits.

Soybeans -Glycine max- are a legume native to East Asia, cultivated for thousands of years and now grown extensively worldwide, including major production regions in the Americas, East Asia, and South Asia. Their flavor is mild and slightly nutty, adapting well to countless preparations. Soybeans are among the most versatile and widely used legumes globally, forming the basis of foods like tofu, soy milk, soy sauce, miso, tempeh, edamame, and soybean oil, as well as animal feed. Nutritionally, they are notable for their high plant protein content, along with dietary fiber, healthy fats, and various vitamins and minerals.
SOYBEAN OIL is a vegetable oil extracted from the seeds of the soybean -Glycine max-.

Spelt is an ancient wheat variety that originated in the Near East and was widely cultivated across Europe, particularly Germany and Switzerland, from the Bronze Age until being largely displaced by modern wheat. It has a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor with a tender yet chewy texture, used much like wheat in bread, pasta, and baked goods, often prized for its more digestible protein structure. Spelt does contain gluten and offers a good source of fiber, protein, manganese, and B vitamins, along with more zinc and iron than common wheat.

Spirulina is a blue-green algae -cyanobacterium- that's grown and processed as a food and dietary supplement. Very high in protein -roughly 55–70% by dry weight-, including all essential amino acids. Rich in B vitamins -especially B12-like compounds, though its B12 isn't well-absorbed by humans-, iron, and antioxidants like phycocyanin -the pigment giving it its blue-green color-. It contains omega-6 fatty acids -notably gamma-linolenic acid-

Stabilisers are substances which make it possible to maintain the physico-chemical state of a foodstuff; stabilisers include substances which enable the maintenance of a homogenous dispersion of two or more immiscible substances in a foodstuff, substances which stabilise, retain or intensify an existing colour of a foodstuff and substances which increase the binding capacity of the food, including the formation of cross-links between proteins enabling the binding of food pieces into re-constituted food.
STARCH is a polymeric carbohydrate consisting of a large number of glucose units joined by glycosidic bonds.
Root vegetable with a significant amount of starch.

STREPTOCOCCUS THERMOPHILUS also known as Streptococcus salivarius subsp. thermophilus is a gram-positive bacterium, and a fermentative facultative anaerobe, of the viridans group. It is also classified as a lactic acid bacterium.

Sucrose is a disaccharide composed of glucose and fructose, occurring naturally in many plants but concentrated commercially from sugarcane and sugar beet—the two primary sources refined into the table sugar found worldwide. It has a pure, intensely sweet flavor with no notable aroma, forming the chemical basis for the many refined sugar products -granulated, powdered, brown, etc.- that vary mainly in processing rather than composition. Used universally as a sweetener in food and beverages, sucrose provides purely empty calories with no meaningful vitamins, minerals, or fiber, serving as a source of energy without nutritional value.

Sugar -sucrose- comes from sugarcane, first domesticated in New Guinea thousands of years ago and later spread through Asia and the Middle East to become the dominant global source, and from sugar beet, which took hold in Europe after Napoleon's early 1800s Continental Blockade cut off cane sugar imports and spurred domestic beet production, making it the region's primary source today. It has a pure, intensely sweet flavor with no notable aroma, available in forms ranging from fine granulated and powdered sugar to coarser raw and brown sugars with mild molasses notes. Used universally in baking, cooking, preserving, and sweetening beverages, sugar provides purely empty calories with no meaningful vitamins, minerals, or fiber, making it a source of energy without nutritional value.
SULTANA is a "white" -pale green-, oval seedless grape variety also called the sultanina, Thompson Seedless, Lady de Coverly, and oval-fruited Kishmish.
SUNFLOWER OIL is the non-volatile oil pressed from the seeds of sunflower -Helianthus annuus-.

A sweet potato is a starchy root vegetable. It grows underground as a swollen root, It's skin can be orange, purple, white, or reddish; flesh is often orange, but also comes in white or purple. It has a naturally sweet flavor, especially when roasted or baked. It is rich in beta-carotene -converts to vitamin A- and a good source of fiber, vitamin C, potassium, and manganese, and has complex carbohydrates, so it digests more slowly than many other starches
Sweeteners are substances used to impart a sweet taste to foods or in table-top sweeteners.

SYRUP is a condiment that is a thick, viscous liquid consisting primarily of a solution of sugar in water, containing a large amount of dissolved sugars but showing little tendency to deposit crystals.
TAPIOCA is a starch extracted from cassava root -tapioca seems to be the same as tapioca starch, but not used as such on ingredient lists-

Taurine is an organic compound that is widely distributed in animal tissues. Taurine has many fundamental biological roles. Taurine is a common additive to energy drinks, which are often promoted as such.
Thiamine, also known as thiamin or vitamin B1, is a vitamin found in food, and manufactured as a dietary supplement and medication.
Thickeners are substances which increase the viscosity of a foodstuff.
A tortilla is a type of thin flatbread, typically made from nixtamalized corn or wheat flour.

Triticale is a hybrid grain bred by crossing wheat and rye, first developed in the late 19th century and refined for commercial use in Europe through the 20th century. Its flour has an earthy, nutty flavor that combines wheat's mildness with rye's slight tanginess. It's used to make breads, pastas, and crackers, often blended with other flours for improved texture and rise. Nutritionally, whole-grain triticale flour is high in fiber, protein, and minerals like magnesium and iron, though it still contains gluten.

A TRUFFLE is the fruiting body of a subterranean ascomycete fungus, predominantly one of the many species of the genus Tuber. In addition to Tuber, many other genera of fungi are classified as truffles including Geopora, Peziza, Choiromyces, Leucangium, and over a hundred others.

A tuber is a swollen underground stem -or in some cases a swollen root-, used for storing nutrients — like potatoes. It typically grows at the end of a rhizome or stolon, not as the plant's central root.
TURMERIC is a flowering plant of the ginger family, Zingiberaceae, the roots of which are used in cooking. Note that turmeric contains some curcumine -E100-.
Vanillin is a phenolic aldehyde, which is an organic compound with the molecular formula C8H8O3.
In common usage, vegetable oil may refer exclusively to vegetable fats which are liquid at room temperature
VEGETABLE OILS, or vegetable fats, are fats extracted from seeds, or less often, from other parts of fruits.
VINAIGRE is a liquid consisting of about 5–20% acetic acid -CH3COOH-, water -H2O-, and trace chemicals that may include flavorings.

Vital wheat gluten is a concentrated protein extracted from wheat flour by washing away the starch, a process refined industrially in the 20th century to create a versatile baking additive. On its own it's bland and neutral in flavor, though it develops a chewy, meaty texture when hydrated and cooked. It's used to boost elasticity and rise in bread dough, and is a key ingredient in seitan and other plant-based meat substitutes. Nutritionally, it's exceptionally high in protein -over 75%- with very little fat or carbohydrate, though as pure gluten it's unsuitable for those with gluten intolerance or celiac disease.
A walnut is the nut of any tree of the genus Juglans. After full ripening for its edible seed when the shell has been discarded, it is used as a garnish or a snack.

Water is a naturally occurring compound of hydrogen and oxygen, found throughout the environment in oceans, rivers, lakes, and groundwater, and sourced for consumption from municipal supplies, wells, springs, and glaciers depending on region. It has a neutral, essentially flavorless and odorless profile, though mineral content can lend subtle differences—spring water often tastes slightly mineral-rich, while distilled water tastes notably flat. As the foundation of virtually all food and beverage preparation, water contains no calories, protein, fat, or carbohydrates, though mineral or spring varieties may carry trace amounts of minerals like calcium, magnesium, and potassium, and it remains essential for nearly every bodily function.
WHEAT is a grass widely cultivated for its seed.

Wheat flour comes from wheat, one of the world's oldest cultivated grains, first domesticated in the Fertile Crescent around 10‚000 years ago and now the dominant grain in global bread-making, especially in Europe, the Middle East, and the Americas. It has a mild, slightly sweet, neutral flavor with a texture that ranges from soft and fine -cake flour- to coarse and hearty -whole wheat-, largely defined by its protein and gluten content, which gives dough its characteristic elasticity and chew. Wheat flour contains gluten and, depending on whether it's whole grain or refined, provides varying levels of fiber, B vitamins, iron, and protein—whole wheat retaining significantly more nutrients since the bran and germ aren't stripped away.

WHEAT GERM is a concentrated source of several essential nutrients, including vitamin E, folate -folic acid-, phosphorus, thiamin, zinc, and magnesium, as well as essential fatty acids and fatty alcohols. It is a good source of fiber. Wheat germ can be added to protein shakes, casseroles, muffins, pancakes, cereals, yogurt, smoothies, cookies, and other goods.

Suji -semolina- is a coarsely milled wheat product, made by grinding the hard endosperm of wheat -often durum wheat- into granular particles, with bran and germ largely removed — similar refinement to maida but coarser in texture. Used across the Mediterranean and South Asia for centuries, it has a mild, slightly nutty taste and a distinctive grainy, granular texture that gives dishes a light, fluffy bite. Used for upma, sheera/halwa, dosa batter, idli, pasta, and as a coating for frying. Nutritionally, it's calorie-dense with moderate protein, but low in fiber like maida, retaining few micronutrients from the removed bran and germ.
WHEY is the liquid remaining after milk has been curdled and strained.
WHEY PROTEIN is a mixture of globular proteins isolated from whey, the liquid material created as a by-product of cheese production.

Whipping cream is a high-fat dairy product -typically 30–36% milk fat- that, when chilled and beaten, traps air to form soft or stiff peaks. It is lightly sweetened for desserts, holds its shape for piping, and adds a rich, velvety mouthfeel to mousses, ganaches, and sauces. Because of its lower fat content than heavy cream, it whips faster but is less stable over time.

White corn is from the whole kernel of white corn — a corn variety that lacks the yellow/orange carotenoid pigments found in standard yellow corn. it's very similar to whole-grain yellow corn flour in calories, protein, and fiber — the main practical difference is the near-absence of vitamin A precursors.
Xylanase is any of a class of enzymes that degrade the linear polysaccharide xylan into xylose,[1] thus breaking down hemicellulose, one of the major components of plant cell walls.

Yeast is a single-celled fungus, most commonly Saccharomyces cerevisiae, used for thousands of years since ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian times to leaven bread and ferment beverages like beer and wine, long before its microbial nature was understood. It has a mild, slightly savory, umami flavor with a subtly yeasty, bread-like aroma, and comes in fresh, active dry, or instant forms that vary in texture from soft and crumbly to fine granules. Used in baking, brewing, and winemaking, yeast works by converting sugars into carbon dioxide and alcohol through fermentation, and nutritional yeast -a deactivated form- is notably rich in B vitamins, protein, and often fortified with B12, making it a popular supplement for plant-based diets.

Yeast extract is a savory paste or powder made by breaking down yeast cells—typically through autolysis -self-digestion using the yeast's own enzymes- or hydrolysis—a byproduct process refined in the late 19th century that led to iconic products like Marmite in the UK and Vegemite in Australia. It has an intensely savory, salty, umami-rich flavor with deep, almost meaty notes, and comes as a thick, sticky spread or dried into a fine powder used as a seasoning. Used as a flavor enhancer in soups, sauces, stocks, and spreads, yeast extract is naturally rich in glutamic acid -contributing its umami punch-, B vitamins, and protein, making it both a flavor booster and a modest nutritional contributor.

Yellow corn is from the whole kernel of yellow corn, the most common corn type used in the US. Yellow corn gets its color from carotenoids, including beta-carotene, which the body can convert to vitamin A — so unlike white corn flour, yellow corn flour has some vitamin A activity.
ZINC is a chemical element with symbol Zn and atomic number 30.
ZINC OXIDE is an inorganic compound with the formula ZnO. Zinc oxide is added to many food products, including breakfast cereals, as a source of zinc, a necessary nutrient.
ZINC SULFATE has the formula ZnSO4 as well as any of three hydrates. As a supplement it is used to treat zinc deficiency and to prevent the condition in those at high risk.
